case_study_insert.main_stem: Jasper Network Cloud (JNC) is a cooperative in the managed IT support and business broadband sector, employing a workforce of 32. Founded in 2018 by Aroha Ngatai, the business provides 24/7 helpdesk services to small firms and operates a hierarchical structure with democratic leadership. JNC plans to invest $480,000 in a new network operations centre, financed by a $300,000 bank loan and $180,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $192,000 a year, a variable cost of $6.00 a unit and a selling price of $18.00, and currently produces 48,000 units a year. JNC faces two problems: its first-response time has risen to 42 minutes and customer complaints have reached 96 a month.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Operations and Quality Report — Q4 2025: Jasper Network Cloud logged 12,000 support tickets last month with a first-response time of 42 minutes, up from 26 minutes a year earlier. Customer complaints reached 96 a month. A survey of 260 small firms found that 71% rated 24/7 cover as essential and 59% would switch provider after two slow responses. On-the-job coaching by senior technicians costs $280 per trainee; a local college certificate course costs $920 per person.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Profit or Loss and Capital employed data of Jasper Network Cloud for the year ended 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 3.50% to 4.25%, increasing the cost of variable-rate borrowing. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 5.6% from $15.00 to $15.84 per hour from April 2026, lifting wage bills for 24/7 support teams. (3) Broadband wholesale and network-equipment costs have risen 8.7% year-on-year, while IT services inflation is 5.3% and business spending on managed support grew 4.9%.

questions.question_text: JNC must fund its $480,000 network operations centre. Explain two advantages for JNC of using a bank loan rather than waiting to build up more retained profit.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: A bank loan provides the $300,000 needed now, so the network operations centre can be opened immediately and the first-response time of 42 minutes can be cut before more of the 260 surveyed firms act on the 59% who would switch after two slow responses. Waiting to accumulate that sum from retained profit could take years, during which the 96 monthly complaints might damage JNC's reputation as a cooperative dependent on member trust. Speed protects the revenue base that must support the $480,000 investment.

Point 2: The loan preserves the $180,000 of retained profit as a reserve for the 24/7 helpdesk and for on-the-job coaching at $280 per trainee, which directly targets the 42-minute response problem. Interest is a known, budgetable cost that can be planned alongside the $192,000 of annual fixed costs, whereas a sudden equipment failure with no cash reserve could stop the service entirely. Borrowing also allows JNC to spread the cost of the centre over the years in which it generates benefit, rather than tying up all internal funds at once.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to JNC, its financing and its response-time and complaint problems.

questions.question_text: JNC is promoting its new 24/7 support service. Consider national radio advertising, search-engine advertising, or direct mail to existing business clients. Which should JNC choose? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
National radio advertising: Radio can reach many local firms quickly and build awareness of 24/7 cover, which 71% of the 260 surveyed firms call essential. It is cheaper than television and suits a short message. However, much of the audience is outside JNC's service area or not a business buyer, so wastage is high for a cooperative with only 32 staff and fixed costs of $192,000, and radio cannot demonstrate how the new centre will cut the 42-minute response time.

Search-engine advertising: Search ads reach firms at the moment they look for IT support, are measurable and can be changed daily. They can target the 59% who would switch after two slow responses with a faster-response promise, and cost is variable rather than a large fixed commitment against the $480,000 centre. The drawback is competition for common keywords can raise costs, and leads need a quick follow-up call, which a 32-person team must manage.

Direct mail to existing clients: Mailing current business clients is low-cost, precisely targeted and can explain the new network operations centre in detail, helping to reduce the 96 monthly complaints through better communication. It reinforces relationships with members of the cooperative. Its limits are a narrow reach limited to the current list, slow response and low open rates, so it cannot win many new clients on its own.

Recommendation: JNC should choose search-engine advertising as the main channel. It reaches firms with an active need, is measurable and affordable for 32 staff, and directly addresses the 59% switching risk. Radio is rejected as wasteful and untargeted; direct mail is rejected as too narrow for growth, though it should be retained as a low-cost supporting tool to reassure existing clients about the $480,000 investment.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited description of the three promotional options with minimal application to JNC.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of the advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of JNC with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three options in context with a well-justified recommendation explaining why radio and direct mail are rejected.

questions.question_text: JNC's first-response time has risen to 42 minutes and complaints have reached 96 a month. Explain two benefits for JNC of using democratic leadership in its support team.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Democratic leadership invites the technicians who answer the 96 monthly complaints to suggest how the 42-minute first-response time can be reduced, giving practical, front-line ideas that managers in the hierarchical structure may miss. Since 71% of surveyed firms rate 24/7 cover essential, faster answers protect member confidence in the cooperative. Consultation is realistic with a workforce of 32, and staff who help design shift patterns are more likely to support the new network operations centre.

Point 2: Involvement raises motivation and ownership, so technicians take greater responsibility for resolving calls at first contact, cutting repeat complaints and the pressure that pushed response time from 26 to 42 minutes. Higher commitment also reduces staff turnover in a small team where on-the-job coaching costs $280 per trainee. The approach fits JNC's cooperative values and supports the 59% of firms who would switch after slow responses. It must be managed well, however: too much debate can delay urgent decisions while the 42-minute problem persists.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual development linked to JNC's response time, complaints and hierarchical structure.

questions.question_text: JNC must speed up its helpdesk response. Consider on-the-job coaching by senior technicians at $280 per trainee or a local college certificate course at $920 per person. Which should JNC choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
On-the-job coaching: Coaching at the desk is tailored to JNC's own ticketing system and call routines, so it can attack the 42-minute first-response time immediately and help reduce the 96 monthly complaints. At $280 per trainee, the full workforce of 32 costs $8,960, far below the college route. Staff stay productive while learning, knowledge is shared by senior technicians already trusted in the cooperative, and the approach fits a 24/7 service that cannot easily release everyone at once. The drawbacks are that good technicians lose time while coaching, bad habits may spread, and there is no external certificate to show surveyed firms seeking assurance.

Local college course: A certificate at $920 per person gives structured, recognised training and fresh ideas, which could reassure the 59% of firms who would switch after slow responses. For all 32 staff the cost is $29,440, more than three times the coaching option. It takes people off the helpdesk, reducing capacity while the response time is already 42 minutes, and the generic content may not match JNC's systems, so follow-up coaching would still be needed.

Decision: JNC should choose on-the-job coaching as the main method. It is cheaper by $20,480, specific to the helpdesk and avoids losing capacity while complaints stand at 96 a month. The college course is rejected as too costly and disruptive for a cooperative of 32; a few senior technicians could take the certificate later and then coach others, combining recognition with low cost.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two training methods with limited application to JNC.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of the benefits and drawbacks of both methods in the context of JNC.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both methods in context with a justified decision covering cost, relevance and service disruption.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how JNC's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $192,000 ÷ ($18.00 − $6.00) = $192,000 ÷ $12.00 = 16,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 16,000 units a year.
Formula: Labour productivity = Output ÷ Number of workers. Substitution: 48,000 units ÷ 32 workers = 1,500 units per worker. Answer: labour productivity is 1,500 units per worker a year.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways JNC's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. The 16,000-unit break-even point against output of 48,000 units leaves a margin of safety of 32,000 units, showing the helpdesk is profitable and supporting the $480,000 centre.
2. Labour productivity of 1,500 units per worker gives a baseline for judging whether the 42-minute response time is costing capacity; if tickets per worker fall, management can link it to the 96 monthly complaints.
3. Contribution of $12.00 a unit means each extra support contract after break-even adds $12.00 toward repaying the $300,000 bank loan, so managers can set a monthly sales target.
4. Unit cost of $192,000 ÷ 48,000 + $6.00 = $10.00 can be compared with the $18.00 price to assess efficiency; since 71% of surveyed firms value 24/7 cover, JNC can judge whether faster service justifies the cost of the new centre.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 16,000 units | (ii) Labour productivity = 1,500 units per worker | (iii) Four contextual uses explained: margin of safety of 32,000 units; productivity baseline against the 42-minute response; loan targets from the $300,000 facility; and unit-cost benchmarking at $10.00.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method and 1 mark for accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii). 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate JNC's financial performance by calculating the gross profit margin, profit margin and ROCE for 2024 and 2025. Has JNC's financial performance improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Gross Profit Margin 2024 = 60.0%
Gross Profit Margin 2025 = 65.0%
Profit Margin 2024 = 15.0%
Profit Margin 2025 = 17.5%
ROCE 2024 = 18.0%
ROCE 2025 = 24.0%

Detailed workings: Gross profit of $432,000 on revenue of $720,000 in 2024 gives 60.0%; gross profit of $624,000 on revenue of $960,000 in 2025 gives 65.0%, a rise of 5.0 percentage points. Operating profit increased from $108,000 to $168,000, so the operating-to-revenue percentage improved from 15.0% to 17.5%. Capital employed grew from $600,000 to $700,000, but the return on capital still rose from 18.0% to 24.0% because operating profit grew faster than the asset base. Cost of sales rose from $288,000 to $336,000 while revenue grew by $240,000, so the direct cost share fell. Interest payable fell from $14,000 to $12,000, helping the cooperative retain more earnings.

Evaluation: All three measures improved, so the conclusion rests on a consistent pattern rather than one figure. The 5.0-point jump in the gross percentage is the strongest feature and suggests JNC is spreading helpdesk delivery costs over more contracts or gaining better broadband terms, useful given 8.7% wholesale-cost inflation. The operating percentage rising by 2.5 points shows the $192,000 fixed costs are being absorbed by growth. Return on capital climbing to 24.0% despite $100,000 more capital employed indicates the new assets are already working harder. However, the 42-minute first-response time and 96 monthly complaints could still push costs up and drive away the 59% of firms who would switch after slow responses, so the gain is not secure. One year of data also cannot prove the improvement is permanent.

Conclusion: JNC's financial performance has improved. Gross profitability, operating profitability and return on capital all rose together despite a larger capital employed and lower interest cost. The main threat is service quality, so management should use the $280 on-the-job coaching to protect the trend while the $480,000 network operations centre becomes fully productive.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or directions of change without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates the three profitability ratios for both years with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate calculations for both years with detailed evaluation of revenue, costs, capital employed and a justified conclusion on whether performance improved.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for JNC of introducing automated call-routing software to cut its 42-minute response time.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: Automated routing can send each call straight to the right technician, cutting the 42-minute first-response time and the 96 monthly complaints without adding to the workforce of 32. Since 71% of the 260 surveyed firms rate 24/7 cover essential and 59% would switch after slow responses, faster answers protect members and justify the $480,000 network operations centre. Automation also lets the helpdesk handle the 12,000 monthly tickets more evenly, releasing staff to solve complex problems rather than triage calls.

Disadvantage: Purchase and integration costs add to JNC's $192,000 of annual fixed costs and compete with the $300,000 bank loan. A poorly configured router could send callers to the wrong queue and make the 42-minute problem worse, while a purely automated greeting may frustrate small-firm clients who value personal service. Technicians may also feel displaced by the system, reducing the motivation that democratic leadership is trying to build, and the 12,000-ticket volume means any downtime during installation would immediately increase the 96 complaints.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to JNC's response data, survey and costs.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 4.25%, the 5.6% minimum wage increase and the 8.7% rise in broadband costs will affect JNC. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (from 3.50% to 4.25%): If JNC's $300,000 bank loan carries a variable rate, the additional interest is 0.75% × $300,000 = $2,250 a year (0.0075 × $300,000 = 2,250). This is modest against $192,000 of annual fixed costs, and if the loan is fixed-rate the immediate effect is zero. Higher rates could still make future borrowing for the network operations centre more expensive and may cause small-firm clients to cut support spending.

Minimum wage rise (5.6%, to $15.84 per hour): The insert gives a workforce of 32 and output of 48,000 units a year but states no hours worked and no individual pay, so an annual wage bill cannot be invented. The defensible comparison is productivity: 48,000 ÷ 32 = 1,500 units per worker. If that is sustained, the rise can be absorbed through the $12.00 contribution per unit; if the 42-minute response time and 96 complaints absorb labour time, unit labour cost rises and contribution shrinks. No more precise total is supportable from the insert.

Input-cost inflation (8.7%): The $6.00 variable cost is not broken down in the insert, so only a bound can be shown. If the whole variable cost rose 8.7%, the increase is 0.087 × $6.00 = $0.522, about $0.52 per unit; over 48,000 units that is roughly $25,000 a year (48,000 × $0.52). Even a half-size effect around $0.26 a unit would be about $12,500 a year, reducing contribution from $12.00 toward $11.50 and straining the cash available for the $480,000 centre.

Conclusion: The 8.7% rise in broadband and network-equipment costs will have the greatest impact. It applies to every one of the 48,000 units and attacks the $12.00 contribution that funds the investment, whereas the interest rise is a calculable $2,250 at most and the wage effect cannot be quantified from the insert. JNC can offset part of it through the 71% of firms who value 24/7 cover, but only if the 42-minute response problem is solved first.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the three external changes with limited application to JNC.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on JNC's costs, revenue or financing in context, with shown working where figures are used.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three changes in the context of JNC with a well-justified judgement that input-cost inflation has the greatest impact and why the other two are smaller.
